With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.
Key takeaways
- Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
- Aaron Boone addressed conflicting media reports regarding Aaron Judge’s status.
- New York projects Gerrit Cole to lead its postseason starting rotation.

The New York Yankees have three main arms in their bullpen who they can rely on during the postseason. This trio of relievers consists of closer David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, the Yankees' best relief assets all season.
But who can they count on in the trust tree behind these three relief pitchers? Let's try to project which bullpen arms the Yankees can lean on in the playoffs from most to least trustworthy.
Yankees' most trustworthy relievers as playoffs approach
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has Bednar, Headrick and Blackburn, who he can go to in the late innings if the team has the lead or is in a tie game. But the Yankees are going to need more than that if they're going to make a deep run.
This is where Will Warren will likely come in as someone that can give the Yankees some key innings in long relief in the playoffs. Warren has not allowed a run in three innings as a reliever this season, and has pitched well as of late overall (2.45 ERA in September).
Hear me out on this next one: If Tim Hill makes the postseason roster, he will step up for the Yankees. Hill has allowed just one earned run across 11.1 playoff innings for the Yankees in the last two years. Since May 31, Hill has seen his ERA balloon from 2.53 to 4.71. But he is postseason tested, which means Boone and the Yankees should be able to count on him.
Last but not least, the sixth most trustworthy bullpen option could be newcomer John Schreiber. The right-hander has a 2.00 ERA over nine innings since joining the Yankees at the beginning of the month. Like Hill, Schreiber has postseason success, posting five scoreless relief appearances against the Yankees, ironically, in the 2024 postseason while pitching for the Kansas City Royals.
Who the Yankees shouldn't trust in ther playoff bullpen
Now we get to the part, where the names on this list probably should be pitching in lower leverage spots in the postseason. Fernando Cruz would've been included here, but his return is in doubt due to a partially torn UCL in his right elbow. Beyond Cruz, there is a pair of starters who are coming back from injury that likely can't be trusted at this point.
No. 1 is Clarke Schmidt, who just experienced biceps soreness when trying to warm up in the bullpen on Sunday. Schmidt came back from 2025 Tommy John surgery on September 16, but has been limited to one appearance, where he recorded two outs. It's hard to see how he could be high up on the trust tree in the postseason if the Yankees keep him on the playoff roster.
The second starter is Ryan Weathers, who had a breakout season for the Yankees this year. The expectation was that Weathers could be a solid relief option in the playoffs, but he is now unlikely to return in the regular season due to his left forearm flexor strain. It's difficult to envision Weathers coming back healthy at this point and being a trusted reliever in the biggest games of the year.
Should the Yankees choose to go: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Bednar, Headrick, Blackburn, Warren, Hill, Schreiber, Weathers, Schmidt, that would mean there's one more spot available for a pitcher on a 13-man staff. This last slot would come down to: Luis Gil, Michael Fulmer or Ryan Yarbrough.
While Gil has the most upside of the three, he can be erratic with his command at times. He also has a 6.75 ERA for his career in the postseason. Fulmer has a 4.50 ERA since joining the Yankees last month and Yarbrough is better suited to give length when the team is trailing. Whoever the Yankees decide to give the last spot to will be a low leverage option and at the bottom of the trust tree.

Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

NEW YORK (AP) — Drew Rasmussen allowed his only hit in the seventh inning and struck out 11 as the Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees 6-1 on Tuesday in the second game of a day-night doubleheader to clinch their fifth AL East title.
The Rays (96-61) secured home-field advantage throughout the American League playoffs and took their first division crown since 2021, when they won 100 games. Tampa Bay also earned AL East championships in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season along with 2010 and 2008, when the team had its first winning season after entering the league as an expansion franchise in 1998.
Yandy Díaz hit two-run single off reliever John Schreiber in the seventh and had another two-run single in the ninth for his AL-leading 175th hit. Tampa Bay opened a six-game lead over the second-place Yankees (90-67) with five to play.
In the opener, Carlos Rodón allowed three hits in eight sharp innings as New York delayed Tampa Bay's division celebration with a 2-0 victory.
Taylor Walls started the three-run seventh with a bunt single against Max Fried (5-5) when first base was left uncovered. Ryan Vilade hit an RBI groundout in the third after Díaz’s flyball moved runners to second and third.
Rasmussen (16-5) was nine outs from joining Matt Garza as Tampa Bay pitchers with a no-hitter when he gave up a leadoff double to Heliot Ramos on his 97th pitch. Garza held the Detroit Tigers hitless at Tropicana Field on July 26, 2010.
After allowing Ramos’ hit to left field, Rasmussen got the next two outs before walking Jazz Chisholm Jr. on a full count. Kevin Kelly entered and permitted rookie George Lombard Jr.’s RBI single before retiring Austin Wells on a groundout.
Rasmussen threw a career-high 114 pitches, 72 for strikes. He threw first-pitch strikes to 17 of 24 hitters and notched his fourth career double-digit strikeout game.
Rasmussen allowed one hit for the fourth time this year. He also yielded just one hit in six innings against the Yankees on April 12.
Cam Booser and Bryan Baker pitched an inning apiece to finish the three-hitter.
Fried allowed four runs and six hits in 6 2/3 innings.
The Yankees were held to three hits or fewer for the 13th time this year.
Up next
Tampa Bay RHP Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38 ERA) opposes New York RHP Gerrit Cole (9-9, 3.63) on Wednesday night.

The New York Yankees opted not to add any relief pitchers at the MLB trade deadline. Why? Because Ryan Weathers was going to end up in the bullpen, and Clarke Schmidt was due to return.
The Yankees were relying on two pitchers with extensive injury histories to solidify their bullpen in October. What could possibly go wrong?
Well, everything that could have gone wrong has gone wrong for New York.
Weathers suffered an elbow flexor strain last month and has been sidelined ever since. It now doesn't appear that the left-hander will return before the playoffs, leaving his postseason status in jeopardy.
Schmidt? He suffered a setback at the beginning of August due to forearm cramping. He then finally returned last week and pitched all of one game before ultimately succumbing to biceps cramping while warming up in the bullpen over the weekend.
Naturally, New York ruled him out for the contest.
Schmidt said it was precautionary and that he didn't want to push through, but are we really to think that a pitcher who had been sidelined since last summer after undergoing Tommy John surgery and had made a grand total of 30 appearances between 2024 and 2025 is going to magically rebound and be just fine?
Maybe the right-hander really is okay and will be available sooner than we think, but you can't help but feel that Schmidt's playoff status, much like that of Weathers, is now in limbo.
It make Brian Cashman's mind-boggling decision not to acquire relief help last month that much more egregious, and it moves the Yankees even further away from a deep October run, something that was probably already foreign anyway following Aaron Judge's latest trip to the injured list.
Yes, New York picked up John Schreiber on the waiver wire, and he has certainly helped, logging a 2.00 ERA over eight relief appearances. He will almost certainly be on the postseason roster.
But Schreiber alone isn't enough. Not with Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn burning the candle from both ends and Tim Hill turning into a batting practice machine.
Had Weathers and Schmidt remained healthy, there's no question they would have been able to help. It's the fact that Cashman was whimsically relying on it that's so nonsensical.
I've been a big Cashman defender over the years. I think he's been a very good general manager for a long time. But it's becoming harder and harder to defend his decisions.
Just about every other contending team acquired bullpen help at the trade deadline. Apparently, the Yankees were the only ballclub too good to do so.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

More than almost any other New York Yankees playoff run, this October's edition will provide either immediate vindication for Brian Cashman's trade deadline strategy or all-new reasons to directly blame him for the team's failure. It should be fascinating to watch, if you don't actually have much emotional energy invested in the team's well-being. Clarke Schmidt's postgame note on Sunday evening was just another reason to be anxious about the way this bullpen was constructed and the amount of variables therein.
Trade deadline predictions for the Yankees' haul this year were astoundingly easy to make. A catcher, first and foremost. An impact bat, that was obvious. And then two bullpen arms to help save their late-inning core from running aground before the year ended. Maybe one would be a certified ace, a tier below Mason Miller, but still devilish. Maybe another would be a bounce back candidate or a never-was, someone who Matt Blake could unearth. Either way, the choices were many, but the outcome was obvious: CashGod would be trading for some relievers. Plural.
But then the deadline came and went. We weren't disappointed by the quality of the haul, but rather in a whole new way. No catcher? No relievers? Was this a mistake? Is the deadline tomorrow?
Nope. Cashman went all in and decided that either the prices were too high or not commensurate with the talent available. Instead, he would look the other way and ignore the rising cost of wear-and-tear in August and piece together some bullpen reinforcements using alternate levers. The waiver wire became his friend. His rotation became a plucking ground, as did his own Injured List. Will Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Weathers, Luis Gil, Will Warren, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer be more valuable together than any names he could've added on Aug. 3? That's the bet. We'll see. I have my doubts, but he has his agenda.
And, in case you weren't already lacking confidence, Schmidt's bicep barked on Sunday and prevented him from entering the game, a game that ace reliever Brent Headrick lit on fire with an average fastball that dipped about a mile and a half below his standard velocity on the season. Hmm. If only he could've been rested during the dog days of summer.
Clarke Schmidt's worrisome postgame comments, Brent Headrick outing vs. Diamondbacks tell the same Yankees story
So, for the record, that's Schmidt - after one MLB outing this year - admitting that, out of precaution, he stopped warming up when his arm barked. His rehab was also halted along the way when he felt forearm cramping on Aug. 4, just one day post-trade deadline. The Yankees getting him back to the MLB level after a summer 2025 Tommy John surgery is remarkable. This is not someone a team should be relying on to cover meaningful postseason innings. And yet.
Headrick's stumble comes in an otherwise phenomenal year, and even as he's lost some gas down the stretch, he's still managed to mostly make things work. He's an expert at limiting inherited runners from scoring, and he's alternated spotless outings with troublesome ones post-deadline. No one knows for certain whether bringing on an experienced seventh-inning guy or two in early August would've prevented the effects of overuse from piling up on Headrick's left arm, but we do know having a viable alternative now could help them deemphasize Headrick if he's struggling to recapture his former glory. Batters hit .345 off him in 15 August games.
That group of alternatives probably doesn't, or shouldn't, include Schmidt, who's hanging on by a thread. Again, it'll be Cashman's crew - Schreiber, Fulmer, Warren, and maybe Weathers, who won't be rehabbing in a regular season game - vs. the field to see who's better equipped for October. Fascinating, if it weren't so presumptuous.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees won't win the American League East after dropping two out of three games to the Arizona Diamondbacks and are now looking at another Wild Card series against the Boston Red Sox. The rest of this season will now be about figuring out their roster heading into October, and this Rays series won't mean much.
There are plenty of questions from fans about what the roster should look like in the final week of the season. And if you're curious about that, reach out to Joseph Randazzo on X or Instagram at @YankeeLibrarian. Fans can ask anything, from questions about bullpen trust trees to what to do with Jazz Chisholm Jr. when he's activated.
The state of the bullpen
Who do you trust in the bullpen outside of Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, and David Bednar?@Mattmann1199 on Instagram
At this point, the two best names behind them are Will Warren and John Schreiber. It's likely that they'll be without Ryan Weathers, and that is the name I would have gone with. Now it's probably Schreiber, but I'm not too convinced about this answer.
Since Luis Gil has been blowing 100 out of the bullpen, they can see what they have in him as a pen arm heading into October. None of these answers inspire much, but they have somehow been one of the best bullpens in baseball.
A returning bat
Where should Jazz Chisholm Jr. play when they activate him@theezratakeshita on Instagram
Chisholm should probably go to second base. Volpe has been okay, but since his big debut against the Colorado Rockies, he has gone 7-for-33. He has two doubles, three stolen bases, and two RBI.
Since Boston has a ton of lefty starters, they can probably start a game with Volpe and then go to Chisholm later. That feels like what the Yankees will do, and it's probably the case if Volpe is scorching the ball. Of course, there is still time for Volpe to make things interesting here.
Judge's World Series dreams
The World Series window for Judge is closing. Might he go without ever winning one?@_not_mikeee on Instagram
That is absolutely on the table. There are some great players who have never won a championship. Dan Marino, Barry Bonds, and Henrik Lundqvist never got their ring. Granted, the Scott Hunter character in Heated Rivalry feels like it's loosely based on mid-2010s Lundqvist, but that might only half-count since it's a work of fiction.
A wild storyline would be the Yankees winning a World Series this year without Judge. Imagine the chaos of his legacy talks if that happens.
Job statuses
Is there a scenario that gets Cash or Boone fired this year?@kirby.phillips7 on Instagram
These questions are always easy to answer. Probably not this year. Cashman will probably go out on his own accord. Boone is the most likely candidate to get fired, but there aren't many teams that are going to axe a manager who kept their team afloat and in postseason contention with the amount of injuries they had. When baseball comes back after the lockout, those two will probably still be here.
Missing the playoffs again might do it for them, but the last time that happened, they stayed. It does feel like they have unlimited security in New York.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

The Yankees hit three homers in Arizona on Saturday and still walked away with an 8-4 loss. Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr. all went deep, which should have been plenty of oxygen for a club trying to chase Tampa Bay.
Instead, Will Warren gave up four earned runs in 4 1/3 innings, John Schreiber gave up two more in the eighth, and the Yankees fell to 89-66. They are six games behind the Rays with a four-game series against Tampa Bay packed into three days starting Tuesday. It is a brutal spot after a game with three home runs on the board.
The Yankees cannot live on solo shots
The frustrating part is not that the Yankees lost a road game in September. It is that they got the type of offensive noise that normally buys a team room to breathe, then gave it all back before the night was over.
Ramos has been a useful part of this group, and Jones brought the kind of power that keeps making the October roster debate complicated. Lombard’s homer was another reminder that the young infield is not going to sit quietly just because the calendar got serious.
None of that changes the larger issue. Three solo shots are not a plan when the pitching staff is handing the other side too many extra chances. The Yankees needed cleaner innings from Warren, and they needed the bullpen to keep the game from turning into a chase.
Tampa Bay is waiting for a mistake
The Rays do not need to make a speech about this series. They have a six-game cushion, while the Yankees have four direct opportunities to cut into it. A six-game gap supplies plenty of urgency on its own.
I am not pretending one series erases everything that came before it. But it can change the temperature fast. A split leaves New York scrambling for help elsewhere, while a big run gives the final week a pulse.
Saturday felt like the kind of game that gets brushed off in July. On September 20, with Tampa Bay next, it landed much harder.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

PHOENIX — Una sola entrada convirtió una serie fuera de casa que los Yankees parecían dispuestos a salvar en una derrota que les acompañó hasta su regreso al Bronx.
El domingo, en el Chase Field, Nueva York llegaba a la parte baja de la quinta con una ventaja de tres carreras. Para cuando terminó la entrada, Nolan Arenado ya había dado la vuelta a las bases, Arizona había anotado cinco veces y los Yankees se habían quedado atrás para siempre, acabando por perder 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-66 y a seis partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, cuando solo quedan siete partidos por jugar. Además, esto puso fin a una gira por Arizona con un balance de 1-2, después de que Nueva York empezara la serie con una victoria por 9-2 y luego perdiera dos veces en partidos que se decidieron en los últimos compases.
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Pero la última semana tiene ahora un carácter de urgencia diferente. Tampa Bay puede hacerse con el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana con una sola victoria en la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium.
El domingo también se prolongó el drástico cambio de rumbo tras el partido inaugural del viernes. El sábado terminó con un jonrón decisivo de Pavin Smith contra Michael Fulmer. El último partido trajo consigo otro fallo del bullpen, pero el mismo perjuicio en la clasificación.
Una entrada de cuatro carreras debería haber cambiado el rumbo de la tarde
Arizona se adelantó en el marcador gracias a un sencillo impulsador de Geraldo Perdomo en la primera entrada. A partir de ahí, Will Warren se asentó en el montículo, impidiendo que los Diamondbacks ampliaran su ventaja hasta la cuarta entrada y dando tiempo a la alineación para atacar a Corbin Burnes.
Ese ataque llegó de repente en la tercera entrada.
Heliot Ramos empató el partido con su decimotercer jonrón. George Lombard Jr. le siguió más adelante en la entrada con un jonrón de dos carreras, el quinto de la temporada.
El batazo de Lombard recorrió, según las estimaciones de Statcast, 424 pies, el jonrón más largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Spencer Jones conectó un jonrón justo después, su undécimo. A continuación, lanzó una bola que se calculó que recorrió 448 pies. Los dos jonrones de los novatos sumaron un total de 872 pies.
Los Yankees habían pasado de ir perdiendo 1-0 a ponerse 4-1 por delante y habían obligado a Burnes a abandonar el partido tras solo 2 2/3 entradas. Parecía el tipo de remontada de los jóvenes que podría sacar adelante a una alineación en la que faltaban los titulares lesionados.
En cambio, esas cuatro carreras fueron toda la producción ofensiva de los Yankees.
Diecinueve outs demuestran lo mucho que ha dado un giro el partido
Cinco relevos de los Diamondbacks sumaron entre todos 6 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras tras la salida de Burnes. Los Yankees solo consiguieron tres hits contra ese grupo y no anotaron en las últimas 19 eliminaciones.
Justin Martínez lanzó una quinta entrada sin permitir carreras y se llevó la victoria, mejorando su balance a 3-0. Brent Headrick cargó con la derrota, quedando con un balance de 7-4. No se concedió ningún salvamento.
Los Yankees terminaron el día con 216 jonrones, liderando la Liga Americana, pero su poderío no pudo compensar el colapso que vino después.
Warren y Headrick pierden el quinto
Warren llegó a la quinta entrada defendiendo la ventaja de 4-1. Lars Nootbaar conectó un doble, Ketel Marte un sencillo y Gabriel Moreno recibió una base por bolas, llenando las bases con un out. Aaron Boone recurrió a Brent Headrick, uno de los lanzadores del bullpen más utilizados por los Yankees.
Headrick ponchó a Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas, dejando el marcador en 4-2. Arenado mandó una bola rápida justo fuera por la línea del jardín izquierdo antes de conectar con fuerza el siguiente lanzamiento para un grand slam, dando a Arizona una ventaja de 6-4.
Headrick disputaba su 79.ª salida, la segunda cifra más alta de las Grandes Ligas, y, según se informó, la velocidad media de su bola rápida estaba aproximadamente 1,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Headrick dijo que el problema era la precisión, no el cansancio.
«Me sentí bien, pero me faltó precisión y me quedé atrás respecto a los bateadores», dijo Headrick.
Warren se fue del partido con cuatro carreras encajadas, seis hits y tres bases por bolas en 4 1/3 entradas. Boone ha dicho que Warren hará una salida más como titular en la temporada regular contra Baltimore antes de pasar al bullpen en octubre.
Warren apoyó al relevo que se hizo cargo de la situación complicada que él había dejado.
«Nos ha dado un montón de problemas todo el año», dijo Warren. «Es un rollo, pero está claro que contamos con él, y nos ha ido muy bien con él todo el año, y va a seguir haciéndolo bien».
Arizona sigue sumando mientras el bullpen de los Yankees flaquea
Perdomo impulsó una carrera con un triple ante John Schreiber en la séptima entrada, y Carroll le siguió con un sencillo impulsor que dejó el marcador final en 8-4. Arizona terminó con siete carreras sin respuesta y se aseguró su 47.ª victoria tras remontada, la mejor marca de la MLB.
Los Yankees también se quedaron sin poder ver a Clarke Schmidt en el bullpen, como tenían previsto. El lanzador diestro tuvo que dejar de calentar por unos calambres cerca del brazo que se le había operado. Las primeras pruebas de fuerza fueron alentadoras, y se esperaba que Schmidt fuera examinado una vez que el equipo volviera a Nueva York.
Por qué esta podría ser la derrota más cara de los Yankees en 2026
Tras dos derrotas seguidas en Arizona, los Yankees vuelven al Yankee Stadium con Tampa Bay en condiciones de zanjar la lucha por el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana en el campo de Nueva York.
El daño va más allá de haber desperdiciado una ventaja. El Tampa Bay llega ahora al Bronx y solo necesita una victoria en la doble jornada del martes para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana, ya que esa victoria también le garantizaría el desempate en la serie de la temporada.
Eso da lugar a la consecuencia más incómoda del colapso de Arizona: los Yankees podrían verse obligados a ver cómo los Rays celebran el título de división en el Yankee Stadium, en el mismo campo donde Nueva York esperaba mantener viva la lucha hasta la última semana.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

Brent Headrick served up a grand slam to Nolan Arenado in the fifth inning, flipping the game on its head and all but wrapping up the Yankees’ spot in the AL wild-card series next week after an 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
By dropping the series finale, a game they once led 4-1, the Yankees (89-66) fell to six games back of the Rays with seven to play.
They will welcome the Rays to Yankee Stadium on Tuesday for a four-game showdown, needing a sweep to stay alive in the division race. One win by the Rays in The Bronx will secure them the AL East title.
The Yankees would then turn their attention to securing the top AL wild card, ending Sunday leading the Red Sox by 5 ¹/₂ games, though Aaron Judge’s questionable status for that series because of a calf strain looms over everything.
In the meantime, Sunday’s loss — on the heels of Saturday’s walk-off win by the Diamondbacks (82-74) — was another regrettable one after third-inning home runs by Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones had staked them to a 4-1 lead.
In the bottom of the fifth, Will Warren loaded the bases with one out, at which point Aaron Boone called on reliable lefty Headrick for his 79th appearance of the season — the second most in the majors.
Before Sunday, Headrick had inherited 50 runners this season and allowed only five of them to score.
But after striking out the first batter he faced, Headrick walked Corbin Carroll to force in a run, which brought Arenado to the plate.

In the final game and rubber match of their three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74), the Yankees (89-66) coughed up an early lead to lose 8-4.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Will Warren got the nod to start the game, and delivered a solid outing... until the fifth inning. Up to that point, Warren had allowed one earned run - an RBI single in the first inning by Diamondbacks shortstop Geraldo Perdomo - and struck out four batters through four full innings. The Yankees entered the fifth inning leading 4-1 (thanks to home runs from Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr., and Spencer Jones), but after Warren surrendered two hits and a walk to load the bases with just one man out, he was pulled in favor of left-handed reliever Brent Headrick.
-- Headrick struck out Perdomo to record the second out, but he couldn't close the door on the frame, issuing a free pass to Corbin Carroll to bring in one run before surrendering a grand slam to Nolan Arenado which gave Arizona a 6-4 lead.
-- Of those five earned runs surrendered in the fifth, three were attributed to Warren, and two to Headrick.
-- New York's right-handed reliever John Schreiber allowed two more runs in the seventh inning, surrendering a triple to Perdomo and a single to Carroll which brought the shortstop home. For Arizona, former Yankee Jonathan Loáisiga recorded the final six outs, facing the minimum six batters without allowing a run to wrap up the 8-4 loss.
Game MVP: Nolan Arenado
Arenado's grand slam flipped the game on its head, and the massive momentum-shifting blast gave the Snakes a lead they wouldn't relinquish.
Highlights
What's next
The Yankees travel back home on Monday and will kick off a pivotal three game series against the AL East divisional leading Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday at 1:05 p.m.
Of course, now 6.0 games back of Tampa Bay for first place in the AL East with just seven regular season games remaining, the Yankees need a miracle to win the division.
Carlos Rodón (2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP in 76.1 IP) is set to take the mound for the Yankees.
The Rays will send out Nick Martinez (2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP in 171.1 IP).

PHOENIX — Los Yankees se han pasado todo el mes de septiembre intentando convertir su clasificación para la postemporada en una plantilla más clara de cara a octubre. Una de sus decisiones más difíciles de tomar ahora mismo tiene que ver con la tercera base.
Ryan McMahon llegó como un jugador que aportaba estabilidad sobre todo en defensa, pero cada vez le cuesta más ocultar su bateo. Su último bache se produjo el miércoles en el Target Field, donde se fue de 0 de 6 con cuatro strikeouts en la derrota por 5-4, en 13 entradas, ante los Minnesota Twins.
Los Yankees no dejaron de remontar. Anthony Volpe empató el partido con un doble en la novena entrada. Ali Sánchez puso a Nueva York por delante en la décima, y José Caballero sumó un fly de sacrificio en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que Víctor Caratini sentenció el partido con un sencillo decisivo en la 13.ª. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, John Schreiber la derrota y no hubo salvamento.
McMahon, que bateaba séptimo, terminó la noche con un promedio de .210/.275/.346, 10 jonrones y 34 carreras impulsadas en 118 partidos. Se ha puesto a cero 101 veces, lo que supone un porcentaje del 29,2 %, mientras que su OPS es de .621. Las estadísticas avanzadas actuales que acompañan a las críticas le sitúan en un wRC+ de 77 y un fWAR de 0,5.
Este momento hace que cada turno al bate sin resultado se note más. Los Yankees llegaban al viernes con un balance de 88-64, a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Jazz Chisholm Jr. sigue en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Volpe ha vuelto de la Triple A y ha jugado como segunda base.
La trayectoria de Volpe en las ligas menores ha ampliado las opciones de los Yankees. Durante su etapa en la Triple A, jugó como shortstop, segunda base y tercera base. Eso no significa que sea la solución definitiva para la tercera base, pero le da a Aaron Boone otra opción de alineación que tener en cuenta cuando vuelva Chisholm.
McMahon también tiene un sueldo garantizado de 16 millones de dólares para 2027. Los Yankees tienen que decidir si su defensa y su contrato siguen justificando que sea titular cuando la diferencia en ataque se ha vuelto tan grande.
McMahon entra en la zona de peligro de LeMahieu
Esa combinación ha hecho que cada vez más gente de los Yankees se plantee una pregunta más dura: si McMahon debería perder su puesto de titular, quedar fuera de la plantilla de la postemporada o, al final, ser designado para cesión.
La comparación que está cobrando fuerza es la de DJ LeMahieu, a quien los Yankees dejaron libre en julio de 2025 cuando aún le quedaban por cobrar unos 22 millones de dólares. Según FanGraphs, en su última temporada con los Yankees, LeMahieu registró un wRC+ de 94, un porcentaje de embasado de 0,338 y una tasa de strikeouts del 24,6 %.
McMahon está por debajo de todos esos indicadores ofensivos. Su porcentaje de llegada a base de 0,275 y su tasa de strikeouts del 29,2 % hacen que los Yankees obtengan menos aportación ofensiva de la que recibían de LeMahieu antes de decidir que ya no encajaba en su plantilla.
Las situaciones no son iguales. LeMahieu tenía 36 años, su papel se había reducido y Nueva York quería a Chisholm en segunda base. McMahon es más joven y sigue aportando valor en tercera base. Pero la decisión sobre LeMahieu dejó claro que el dinero garantizado no siempre protege el puesto de un veterano en la plantilla.
Boone sigue centrándose en el grupo
Los Yankees no han dicho públicamente que McMahon vaya a quedar fuera de la plantilla. Tras asegurarse el título, Boone habló de cómo el vestuario había afrontado una temporada difícil, en lugar de dar a entender que se hubiera tomado ninguna decisión sobre un veterano.
«Pero hay que reconocerles el mérito de haberse mantenido unidos. A pesar de todos los altibajos, han sido un grupo muy unido», dijo Boone.
Ese comentario no aclara cuál será el papel de McMahon en octubre. Lo que sí hace es resaltar la diferencia entre las presiones externas para que lo echen y la decisión que los Yankees hayan tomado realmente.
La defensa ya no es la respuesta definitiva
El argumento más sólido de McMahon sigue siendo su guante. La instantánea que te he pasado muestra un DRS de -1 y un Fielding Run Value de +1, mientras que la página en directo de Statcast muestra un valor defensivo global ligeramente positivo. La cifra exacta varía según la métrica y el momento de la actualización, pero la ventaja defensiva no oculta un OPS de 0,621.
Un tercera base con un OPS de 0,621 puede seguir siendo una opción válida si su defensa es de primera y el resto de la alineación está en forma. Los Yankees tienen menos margen mientras Chisholm esté de baja, y en octubre cada puesto de la alineación cobra más importancia.
Volpe no es un tercera base contrastado en las Grandes Ligas, y los Yankees no han dado a entender que tengan pensado darle esa posición. Aun así, su reciente actuación en esa posición en la Triple A le da a Boone una alternativa real. Su experiencia como campocorto hace que la objeción sobre la potencia de su brazo no sea tan sencilla, pero eso no garantiza que vaya a defender bien la tercera base en octubre.
La comparación de Okamoto hay que ponerla en contexto
Otra comparación que circula entre los aficionados de los Yankees compara a McMahon con el tercera base de Toronto, Kazuma Okamoto. Según la MLB, Okamoto tiene un promedio de bateo de 0,235, con 33 jonrones, 88 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 0,774. Su contrato de cuatro años y 60 millones de dólares tiene un valor medio anual de 15 millones de dólares.
McMahon gana 16 millones de dólares y lleva 10 jonrones con un OPS de 0,621. A primera vista, el contraste es enorme.
No se trata de una decisión de la directiva en la que se pueda comparar a uno con otro sin más. McMahon ya tenía contrato cuando los Yankees lo ficharon en 2025, mientras que Okamoto llegó a la MLB siguiendo un camino diferente como agente libre. Aun así, la comparación salarial ayuda a entender por qué se han intensificado las críticas y por qué algunas de ellas se han extendido hasta el director general, Brian Cashman.
Octubre obliga a los Yankees a decidirse por un papel
No hay indicios confirmados de que los Yankees hayan decidido designar a McMahon para cesión o sacarlo de la plantilla de la postemporada. Sigue en activo, y la incertidumbre sobre la fecha de regreso de Chisholm hace que la situación en el cuadro siga siendo incierta.
Pero la cuestión ya no es si McMahon está pasando por una mala racha. Es cuánto tiempo de juego pueden permitirse los Yankees darle a un bateador con un wRC+ de 77 cuando empiece octubre.
Nueva York comienza este viernes una serie de tres partidos en el Chase Field contra Arizona. McMahon tiene tiempo para cambiar el rumbo, pero los Yankees ahora tienen menos margen de maniobra y más alternativas en el cuadro que hace un mes.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons.
The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh before being removed due to pitch count.
It wasn't the cleanest outing, as he wasn't able to get through a full inning after throwing 24 pitches to four batters, but for someone on a big league mound for the first time in 14 months, you had to like what you saw, striking out a pair and only surrendering a pair of soft-hit singles.
The runway is rather short for the remainder of the season with just 10 games left, but Schmidt will likely see his way into four or so games down the stretch. That gives him a total of five outings to truly figure out where he can fit into a wide-open bullpen trust tree.
Clarke Schmidt's bullpen experience
Converting a full-time starter to the bullpen is not always as easy as it seems, but it's a transition the Yankees will have to make three times as we head into the postseason, with Ryan Weathers' likely return and Will Warren's place in the rotation. That said, Schmidt has a bit of an advantage.
Before becoming a full-time starter at the major-league level in 2023, Schmidt was used almost exclusively as a reliever in his brief big-league stints, most notably in 2022, when he posted a 3.12 ERA in 57.2 innings as part of a makeshift bullpen that got very good results. He didn't get himself high up the totem pole, but he pitched some important innings for the club.
His playoff experience as a reliever was unfortunately one to forget. He was saddled with a pair of losses, first in Game 3 of the ALDS after a squeaker by Oscar Gonzalez got through the infield for a walk-off single, and the second in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Houston Astros, where he allowed home runs to Yuli Gurriel and Chas McCormick in the sixth inning of what would be the start of a sweep.
He was supposed to be in the bullpen the following season, but a mountain of injuries forced him to step up in the rotation, starting what became a nightmarish 2023 season. Since then, Schmidt has made 63 appearances through his season-ending elbow surgery in 2025, all but one as a starter.
That's not in the cards for 2026, so what can he do to be useful for the Yankees in the playoffs?
Where Schmidt could fit into unstable bullpen
Schmidt adds a multi-inning righty option to a bullpen that has a lot of moving parts. He leaned hard on a cutter-slider combo on Wednesday, but also featured his sinker, four-seamer, and curveball. His velocity looked as firm as ever, something that could be enhanced but didn't need to hold back for 100 pitches.
The bullpen's premier multi-inning righty is Paul Blackburn, who relies on a ton of spin and movement in his profile, making him more volatile in games with shoddy command. He, along with closer David Bednar and lefty Brent Headrick, makes up the team's three highest-leverage arms, but it's wide open beneath them, particularly after Fernando Cruz's elbow injury.
John Schreiber has been effective as a righty specialist in a small sample, so he feels like the leader in the clubhouse as the team's sixth-inning arm, but he might not be playable in certain matchups due to his struggles against lefties. Tim Hill's overall struggles, even if he remains sharp against lefties, will also give pause. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil haven't pitched enough to earn trust in leverage.
There are two ways that Schmidt can be deployed. One of which is as the team's right-handed bridge reliever, as sort of a "platoon" with Ryan Yarbrough (or Weathers, when he returns). Lineups with more right-handed hitters will fare significantly better against Weathers or Yarbrough if the team needs them to come into a big spot to provide some length to the back-end guys, so having a guy with the opposite hand who can fill that role is valuable.
But that role could be reserved for Warren, who's more stretched out than Schmidt and isn't at risk of being removed due to a long inning. I doubt Schmidt would be permitted to throw much more than 30 pitches in a game. That could lead the 30-year-old to be more in the Schreiber role as the sixth-inning guy, possibly pitching in higher leverage if needed due to overuse.
There are a lot of questions about Schmidt as we come down the stretch, but the important thing is that he's back and he's healthy. The more bullpen depth, the merrier.

On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Carlos Rodón lanzó seis entradas para los Yankees el miércoles y evitó que se les escapara una tarde complicada, pero las estadísticas finales no lo dicen todo. El zurdo cedió dos carreras y cuatro hits, concedió tres bases por bolas y ponchó a cinco en 102 lanzamientos , en la derrota por 5-4 de Nueva York, en la 13.ª entrada, ante los Minnesota Twins en el Target Field.
Rodón se fue del partido con los Yankees perdiendo por 2-0. Anthony Volpe igualó el marcador con un doble de dos carreras en la novena entrada, y Nueva York se puso por delante tanto en la décima como en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que un sencillo de Víctor Caratini, como bateador suplente, puso fin al partido en la decimotercera entrada. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, mientras que John Schreiber se llevó la derrota.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 88-64. Tampa Bay ganó más tarde ese mismo miércoles, lo que deja a Nueva York a 4,5 partidos de los Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero las decisiones que tengan que tomar ahora sobre la rotación de lanzadores tendrán repercusiones en la clasificación de la división y en el orden de salida en octubre.
Los resultados de Rodón siguen siendo sólidos. El miércoles sumó su 25.ª salida consecutiva en la que ha cedido tres carreras limpias o menos, todo un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees. Además, ha encadenado dos salidas de calidad seguidas y ha logrado su quinta salida de calidad en 15 partidos, después de haber lanzado 6 1/3 entradas contra los Mets en su anterior salida.
Su carga de trabajo también ha ido por buen camino. Rodon lanzó 102 lanzamientos el miércoles, su mejor marca de la temporada, tras haber llegado a los 93 lanzamientos contra los Mets. Desde que volvió de la lista de lesionados a mediados de agosto, tiene una efectividad de 2,40, un WHIP de 0,93 y una relación de 31 ponches por cada 12 bases por bolas en 30 entradas.
Para los Yankees, sin embargo, la pregunta que surge tras la visita a Minnesota no es si Rodon podrá aguantar una salida. Es si podrá recuperar su potencia habitual lo suficientemente rápido, ahora que las alineaciones de octubre dejan menos margen para una puesta en marcha gradual.
El calendario deja a los Yankees poco tiempo para distinguir entre una fluctuación temporal y una tendencia que se repita.
Los primeros 55 lanzamientos cuentan una historia diferente
La preocupación se notó desde el principio en todo el repertorio de lanzamientos de Rodon, no solo en su bola rápida de cuatro costuras. La instantánea del seguimiento de lanzamientos adjunta a la salida mostraba que sus cinco lanzamientos estaban por debajo de su velocidad media de la temporada tras 55 lanzamientos.
Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,6 mph, frente a la media de la temporada de 94,4 mph, lo que supone una caída de 1,8 mph. Su slider bajó 1,4 mph, su cambio de velocidad 2,3 mph, su sinker 1,9 mph y su curva 1,1 mph.
Recurrió a la bola rápida de cuatro costuras en el 45 % de esos primeros 55 lanzamientos y al slider en el 29 %. Eso significa que casi tres cuartas partes de su repertorio inicial procedían de dos lanzamientos que estaban 1,8 mph y 1,4 mph por debajo de sus valores habituales de la temporada.
Eso hace que esa caída inicial sea más notable que el dato de una sola bola rápida. El cambio de velocidad fue el que mostró la mayor diferencia, mientras que ambos tipos de bola rápida estaban casi 2 mph por debajo de sus niveles anuales.
Pero Rodon no se quedó ahí. Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,3 mph en la primera entrada, 92,8 en la segunda y 92,4 en la tercera. En la cuarta, esa media subió a 94,9 mph, y más tarde lanzó varios lanzamientos por encima de las 95 mph.
Rodon necesitaba tiempo para soltarse un poco
Rodon habló después sobre su mal comienzo. La información disponible tras el partido no especificaba que esa rigidez se debiera a su codo. Describió cómo se sentía al principio, antes de que su velocidad mejorara a medida que avanzaba el partido.
Rodon dijo que empezó el partido un poco «tenso» antes de soltarse.
Esa formulación es importante por su historial médico de 2026. Rodon empezó la temporada en la lista de lesionados tras someterse a una operación durante la pretemporada para extirparle un espolón óseo del codo izquierdo. Más tarde volvió a la lista de lesionados por una inflamación en el codo izquierdo y se reincorporó el 18 de agosto tras un periodo de rehabilitación.
No se determinó que esa molestia fuera un problema en el codo, y no se informó de ninguna nueva lesión de Rodon tras el partido. Aun así, los Yankees tendrán motivos para estar atentos a la rapidez con la que recupere su velocidad en su próxima salida, tras una temporada acortada por las lesiones.
Los buenos resultados están ocultando una carga de trabajo más intensa
La eficacia de Rodón se ha mantenido intacta, aunque la forma de llegar a las seis entradas haya cambiado. Contra los Mets, el 11 de septiembre, necesitó 93 lanzamientos para completar 6 1/3 entradas, concedió una base por bolas y ponchó a ocho. Cinco días después, necesitó 102 lanzamientos para completar seis entradas, con tres bases por bolas y cinco ponches.
De los 102 lanzamientos del miércoles, solo 59 fueron strikes, algo menos del 58 %. Aun así, limitó a Minnesota a cuatro hits y dos carreras, pero el mayor número de corredores en base y los conteos más ajustados hicieron que esta salida le costara más esfuerzo que su anterior salida.
Teniendo en cuenta sus estadísticas de la temporada hasta el miércoles y su actuación final contra Minnesota, Rodon tiene ahora una ERA de aproximadamente 2,95 en 76 1/3 entradas repartidas en 15 salidas como titular. Los Yankees han contado con él para evitar que el rival anote cuando ha estado disponible.
La salida de los Rays sube el listón
Se espera que la próxima salida de Rodón sea durante la serie de cuatro partidos en casa de los Yankeescontra Tampa Bay, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida en el Yankee Stadium. Nueva York lleva un balance de 3-6 contra los Rays esta temporada.
Ese partido podría ser su última salida como titular en la temporada regular. Además, les da a los Yankees la oportunidad de comprobar directamente si la caída en la velocidad de los lanzamientos del miércoles fue algo puntual o algo que le va a acompañar a Rodon en la postemporada.
Los Yankees obtendrán su siguiente dato cuando le toque lanzar a Rodon contra Tampa Bay, con la lucha por el título de división y la rotación de la postemporada aún en juego.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

El panameño José Caballero volvió a tener incidencia ofensiva, pero no pudo evitar la derrota de los Yankees de Nueva York, que cayeron 5-4 ante los Mellizos de Minnesota en el Target Field, en 13 entradas.
Caballero participó en dos momentos clave del partido. En la novena entrada, anotó una de las carreras del empate tras un doble de Anthony Volpe al jardín derecho, en una jugada en la que también cruzó el plato George Lombard Jr., para mantener con vida a los neoyorquinos.
Más adelante, en la undécima entrada, el infielder istmeño volvió a responder al conectar un elevado de sacrificio al jardín central que remolcó a Lombard Jr., dándole momentáneamente la ventaja 4-3 a los Yankees.
Sin embargo, Minnesota reaccionó en la parte baja de la decimotercera entrada para sellar la victoria y dejar en el terreno al conjunto del Bronx.
Caballero terminó el encuentro sin turnos oficiales, pero con una carrera impulsada y otra anotada. Tras esta actuación, dejó su promedio ofensivo en .234, con 14 cuadrangulares y 51 carreras impulsadas en 129 partidos.
En el montículo, John Schreiber cargó con la derrota al permitir la carrera decisiva en un episodio de labor, en el que concedió un imparable. El triunfo fue para Tommy Nance, quien lanzó una entrada perfecta con dos ponches.
Con el resultado, los Yankees quedan con marca de 88-64, mientras que los Mellizos mejoran a 71-81.
